title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 86
paragraphs: Thus the Athenians say it came about. But the Aeginetans say that it was not with a single ship that the Athenians came; for a single ship, and even a few more than one, they could easily have repelled even if they had had no ships of their own. Rather, they say, the Athenians sailed against their country with a large fleet, and the Aeginetans gave way before them and did not fight a sea-battle. They cannot, however, declare for certain whether they yielded in this way because they admitted they were not strong enough to fight the battle at sea, or because they intended to do something of the kind they actually did. The Athenians then, they say, since no one met them in fight, disembarked from their ships and made for the images; but being unable to tear them up from their pedestals, at last they threw ropes around them and began to pull—until the images, as they were being pulled, both did the same thing (and here they report something which I cannot believe, though another man may): they say the images fell on their knees before them, and that they have remained in that position ever since. The Athenians, they say, were doing this; and meanwhile they themselves (so the Aeginetans say), having been informed that the Athenians were about to make an expedition against them, had brought in the Argives to help them; and just as the Athenians had disembarked on Aeginetan land, the Argives had come to their rescue—and having crossed unnoticed from Epidaurus to the island, they fell upon the Athenians before these had heard anything of the matter, cutting them off secretly from the way back to their ships. And it was at this moment that the thunder and the earthquake came upon them.
